nodes.label: eq:isIn

nodes.name: Initialize poles
nodes.statement: Set the $z'_n$ to the initial guess, as explained in Section~\ref{ssec:initial}.
nodes.statement_short: Initial poles from the Section 2.3 heuristic.

nodes.name: Iterate until stopping criterion
nodes.statement:
\WHILE {stopping criterion not met}
\STATE Solve~\eqref{eq:normalEquations} for the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$. Use only $z'_n \notin \Omega$.
\STATE Use the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$ to form $\widehat{V}$ according to~\eqref{eq:approxV} and $\widehat{W}$ according to~\eqref{eq:compPotToApprox}.
\STATE Form $\widehat{Q}$ according to~\eqref{eq:QHat}, use all $z'_n$.
\STATE Solve~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} for $P$ and $Q$.
\STATE $z'_n = \text{roots}(Q)$.

nodes.name: Solve normal equations for residues
nodes.statement: Solve~\eqref{eq:normalEquations} for the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$. Use only $z'_n \notin \Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares residues using only poles outside $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Form conjugate and complex potential
nodes.statement: Use the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$ to form $\widehat{V}$ according to~\eqref{eq:approxV} and $\widehat{W}$ according to~\eqref{eq:compPotToApprox}.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\widehat V$ and $\widehat W$ from the residues.

nodes.name: Form Q-hat from all poles
nodes.statement: Form $\widehat{Q}$ according to~\eqref{eq:QHat}, use all $z'_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\widehat Q$ from all current poles.

nodes.name: Solve rational-fitting conditions
nodes.statement: Solve~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} for $P$ and $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the linearized rational fit for $P$ and $Q$.

nodes.name: Relocate poles to roots of Q
nodes.statement: $z'_n = \text{roots}(Q)$.

nodes.name: Take roots of Q
nodes.statement: Once $Q(z)$ is obtained, its roots are computed and they become the poles for the next iteration.
nodes.statement_short: Roots of $Q$ become the new poles.

nodes.name: Recompute residues
nodes.statement: Using these poles, $\widehat{U}(z)$, the approximate solution of~\eqref{eq:dirichlet}, is recomputed by solving~\eqref{eq:normalEquations} and then using~\eqref{eq:approxU}.
nodes.statement_short: Recompute residues and $\widehat U$ with the new poles.

nodes.name: Update W-hat and refit
nodes.statement: Similarly, using~\eqref{eq:approxV}, $\widehat{V}(z)$ is recomputed, $\widehat{W}(z)$ in~\eqref{eq:compPotToApprox} is updated, and the poles are relocated again.
nodes.statement_short: Update $\widehat V$, $\widehat W$ and relocate poles again.

nodes.name: Exclude interior poles
nodes.statement: When computing the roots of $Q(z)$ we may encounter roots inside $\Omega$. Although we do not discard these poles, their corresponding basis functions are not used to form $\widehat{U}(z)$ and $\widehat{V}(z)$. Hence, they are tacitly excluded from~\eqref{eq:approxU}-\eqref{eq:normalEquations}.
nodes.statement_short: Interior poles are kept but excluded from the basis.

nodes.name: Discard remaining interior poles
nodes.statement: As the algorithm progresses, these poles usually migrate outside of $\Omega$. Any poles that remain in $\Omega$ when the algorithm stops are discarded.
nodes.statement_short: Discard poles still inside at termination.

nodes.name: Degree-2N real fit
nodes.statement: The initial guess for the $z'_n$ is obtained by solving~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} assuming $\widehat{W}(z) = f(z)$, which is purely real, $\widehat{Q}(z) = 1$, and then allowing $P$ and $Q$ to be of degree $2N$.
nodes.statement_short: Fit real data with $\widehat Q=1$ and degree $2N$.

nodes.name: Select N zeros
nodes.statement: Out of the $2N$ zeros of $Q$ we pick $N$ zeros that are outside $\Omega$, and, if there are not enough of these, we supplement them with zeros inside $\Omega$ so that we have $N$ zeros in total.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $N$ zeros outside $\Omega$, padding with interior ones.

nodes.name: Set initial poles
nodes.statement: These $N$ zeros are used as the poles for the first iteration.
nodes.statement_short: Use them as initial poles.

nodes.name: Per-section Rcheb rule
nodes.statement: Once the $\alpha_{lmn}$ are determined, a quadrature rule for each section of the boundary is calculated, in $O(N L_m)$ time, using the Matlab toolbox Rcheb~\cite{van2008algorithm}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute a rule per section with Rcheb.

nodes.name: Concatenate rules
nodes.statement: The rules are then concatenated to obtain a single rule for the entire boundary.
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate into one boundary rule.

nodes.name: Prototype pole function
nodes.statement: As a prototypical rational function we take a third-order pole function, \begin{equation} R_{s_0}(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s-s_0)^3}, \end{equation} as this is the highest pole order that will appear in the integrands, and estimate the error committed in approximating it by a polynomial, as a function of the pole $s_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Use a third-order pole as the prototype integrand.

nodes.name: Elliptical radius of a pole
nodes.statement: The max-norm error of the polynomial that interpolates at Chebyshev nodes is almost minimal and it is the same for all $s_0$ on the ellipse \begin{equation} s(\phi) = \dfrac{\rho e^{i\phi} + \rho^{-1} e^{-i\phi}}{2}, \quad \phi \in [0, 2 \pi], \end{equation} where $\rho>1$ is the so-called \emph{elliptical radius} (see, e.g.,~\cite{trefethen2009approximation}). For any $s_0 \notin [-1, 1]$ we can calculate the elliptical radius corresponding to the ellipse which passes through it, \begin{equation} \rho(s_0) = \max\left(\left|s_0 + \sqrt{s_0^2-1}\right|, \left|s_0 - \sqrt{s_0^2-1}\right|\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Map each pole to its elliptical radius $\rho(s_0)$.

nodes.name: Tabulate degrees
nodes.statement: Although there are bounds for the error in approximating a function such as $R_{s_0}(s)$ by a polynomial, we found it more practical to tabulate the degrees of polynomials that yield approximation errors less than $\epsilon$, for relevant values of $\epsilon$ and $\rho(s_0)$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:chebyErrs}). \begin{figure}[h] \centering {\scalebox{1}{\includegraphics{cheby_errs.eps}}} \caption{Polynomial degree that yields approximations of $R_{s_0}(s)$ with errors less than $\epsilon$, as a function of $\rho$. For $\rho \approx 10$, errors under $10^{-14}$ can be obtained with polynomial degrees under 20.} \end{figure} To obtain these polynomial degrees, we again used the Chebfun system, which truncates a Chebyshev expansion once the expansion coefficients drop sufficiently below $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Tabulate the required polynomial degree versus $\rho$ and $\epsilon$ using Chebfun.

nodes.name: Pruning radius
nodes.statement: The tabulation is then interpolated or extrapolated as necessary so that we can rapidly calculate the optimal $\rho$ beyond which poles can be discarded and replaced by poles at infinity, without incurring errors much larger than $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate the table to get the pruning radius.

nodes.name: Solve constrained system
nodes.statement: On each iteration, we solve \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^{\mathrm{R}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{R}}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^{\mathrm{I}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{I}}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^\Omega_j\right| \approx f(z), \\[1ex] & \text{with } f(z) = f_j(z) \quad \text{for } z \in \Gamma_j,\\ & \mathrm{subject \ to \ } \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j = 0, \end{split} \end{equation} for the $a_n^{\mathrm{R}}$, the $a_n^{\mathrm{I}}$, and the $A_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve for residues and log coefficients with $\sum A_j=0$.

nodes.name: Eliminate A_J
nodes.statement: The condition that the sum of $A_j$'s is zero, needed to ensure the solution is bounded at infinity, can be enforced by eliminating one of the $A_j$, say, $A_{J} = - \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j$. Instead of~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet} we then have, \begin{equation} \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^{\mathrm{R}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{R}}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^{\mathrm{I}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{I}}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| \approx f(z). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Eliminate $A_J$ to enforce boundedness at infinity.

nodes.name: Least-squares solve
nodes.statement: As before, we solve~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet2} by sampling at quadrature nodes, weighting the equation by the square roots of the quadrature weights, and solving the linear system in the least-squares sense.
nodes.statement_short: Weighted least squares at quadrature nodes.

nodes.name: Poles at infinity for log terms
nodes.statement: In contrast to the previous case, however, the inner products involving the logarithmic basis functions will not be integrated exactly. We must therefore add poles at infinity when deriving the quadrature rules for each section of the boundary. Fortunately, the logarithmic singularity is weak, so when the $z^\Omega_j$ are not too close to the boundary, the restriction of the logarithmic term to the boundary curve can be approximated well by piecewise polynomials. The poles at infinity added by the pole-pruning process of Section~\ref{sec:pruning} usually suffice, although extra poles at infinity can be added if necessary.
nodes.statement_short: Add poles at infinity so log terms are integrated well.

nodes.name: Refit W-tilde
nodes.statement: Once~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet2} has been solved, a rational function is fitted to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$, \begin{equation} \widetilde{W}(z) \approx f(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| + i\widehat{V}(z), \quad z \in \bigcup_{j=1}^{J}{\Gamma_j} = \Gamma. \end{equation} The real part is estimated as $f(z)$, the known values of $\mathrm{Re}[W(z)]$ on the boundaries, with the real part of the logarithmic terms subtracted. The estimate for $\mathrm{Im}[\widetilde{W}(z)]$ is $\widehat{V}(z)$, given by~\eqref{eq:approxV}, and it remains as it was for the simply-connected problem when $\widetilde{W}(z)$ and $W(z)$ were the same.
nodes.statement_short: Rational-fit the estimate of $\widetilde W$ on the boundary.

nodes.name: Subtract log terms
nodes.statement: After this subtraction, \begin{equation} \widetilde{f}_j(z) = f_j(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^J_j\right|, \end{equation} can be used to write a Neumann boundary condition for $\mathrm{Re}\left[\widetilde{W}(z)\right]$. Denoting $\widetilde{W}(z) = \widetilde{U}(z) + i \widetilde{V}(z)$, this condition reads, \begin{equation} \left.\dfrac{\partial \widetilde{U}}{\partial n}\right|_{\text{on }\Gamma_j} = \tilde{f}_j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Subtract known log terms to get a Neumann condition for $\widetilde U$.

nodes.name: Integrate to conjugate data
nodes.statement: If $\widetilde{W}(z)$ is approximated by a weighted combination of dipole potentials, it becomes inconvenient to enforce~\eqref{eq:tildeNeumann} directly, as the differentiation increases the order of the poles. Instead, we integrate~\eqref{eq:tildeNeumann} with respect to arc-length and use the Cauchy-Riemann equations to obtain, \begin{equation} \widetilde{V}(z) = \int_{z_j}^z{ \tilde{f}_j(z)|dz|} + v_j \equiv F_j(z) + v_j, \end{equation} where the integration is along $\Gamma_j$, from an arbitrary point $z_j$ to the point $z$, and the $v_j$ are constants yet to be determined.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate along arc length via Cauchy-Riemann to get Dirichlet data $F_j+v_j$ for $\widetilde V$.

nodes.name: Solve modified Dirichlet system
nodes.statement: Finding a harmonic function $\widetilde{V}$ that satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq:vtilde} is known as a modified Dirichlet~\cite{mikhlin1957integral} or Muskhelishvili~\cite{pogorzelski1966integral} problem, and given the condition at infinity in~\eqref{eq:neumann}, it is solvable only for a unique set of $v_j$ constants. These can be determined along with an approximate solution for $\widetilde{V}$, by solving \begin{equation} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^{\mathrm{R}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{I}}(z) + a_n^{\mathrm{I}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{R}}(z) - v_j \approx F_j(z), \quad \text{for} \ z \in \Gamma_j, \end{equation} for the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$, the $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$, and the $v_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve for residues and the unique constants $v_j$.

nodes.name: Solve and refit
nodes.statement: As before,~\eqref{eq:neumannResidues} is solved in the least-squares sense after sampling the basis functions at quadrature nodes and weighting the equations by the square roots of quadrature weights. Once~\eqref{eq:neumannResidues} is solved, the rational fitting algorithm is applied to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$ given by, \begin{equation} \widetilde{W}(z) \approx \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^{\mathrm{I}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{I}}(z) + a_n^{\mathrm{R}} \phi_n^{\mathrm{R}}(z) + i \left[ F_j(z) + v_j\right], \quad \text{for} \ z \in \Gamma_j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares solve, then rational-fit the estimate of $\widetilde W$.

nodes.name: Local runs
nodes.statement: However, it is still possible to tackle large-scale problems by partitioning the geometry into smaller domains and running the algorithm for each of these domains separately, possibly in parallel.
nodes.statement_short: Run the algorithm per subdomain, possibly in parallel.

nodes.name: Global solve
nodes.statement: Once the poles and testing points are obtained for the entire geometry, we solve the full problem with the locally-optimized poles and testing points.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the full problem with pooled poles and testing points.

nodes.name: Cluster curves
nodes.statement: The scheme consists of partitioning the boundary curves into clusters so that each curve belongs to a single cluster, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:clust}. \begin{figure}[h] \centering \rotatebox{270}{\scalebox{0.4}{\includegraphics{clust.eps}}} \caption{Boundary curves partitioned into three clusters with buffer regions (delimited by dashed lines).} \end{figure} Various algorithms for obtaining such a partition exist, and we use the simplest one, the $k$-means clustering, or Lloyd's, algorithm~\cite{lloyd1982least}. To keep the partitioning simple, each curve is entirely within one cluster and represented by its centroid, on which the clustering algorithm operates.
nodes.statement_short: k-means (Lloyd) clustering of curve centroids.

nodes.name: Add buffer regions
nodes.statement: Then, to each cluster we add a ``buffer region,'' as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:clust}, so that curves close to the edge of the cluster have all their nearby interactions taken into account. The buffer region is obtained by adding to each curve all the curves with centroids closer than some radius, and this radius is chosen as twice the distance to the nearest centroid among all other curves.
nodes.statement_short: Add buffer curves within twice the nearest-centroid distance.

nodes.name: Drop buffer poles
nodes.statement: Poles that, after the local optimization, are found inside the buffer region are not used when solving the full problem.
nodes.statement_short: Drop poles found inside buffer regions.

nodes.name: Stall detection
nodes.statement: A natural possibility is to increase $N$ adaptively, whenever the improvement in accuracy stalls.
nodes.statement_short: Detect stalled accuracy.

nodes.name: Add a pole
nodes.statement: For example, one can calculate $\sigma_K(\Delta E)$, the standard deviation of $\Delta E$ in the previous $K$ iterations, and add a pole whenever \begin{equation} \sigma_K(\Delta E) < \mu_K(\Delta E) \epsilon, \end{equation} where $\mu_K(\Delta E)$ is the $K$-average of $\Delta E$ and $\epsilon$ is a small number.
nodes.statement_short: Add a pole when the error's moving standard deviation is small relative to its mean.

nodes.name: Discretize
nodes.statement: Using the quadrature rules of Section~\ref{ssec:quadForIRF}, we discretize the continuous norm in~\eqref{eq:minProbIRF} and write the minimization problem as, \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}} \, \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=0}^N{ \dfrac{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}{\widehat{Q}(z_k)}\left|{b_n z_k^n - a_n z_k^n \widehat{W}(z_k) }\right|} \end{equation} in which the unknowns are the monomial coefficients of $P(z)$ and $Q(z)$, denoted $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{a}$, respectively. To avoid the trivial solution, a normalization condition, to be specified below, must be imposed on one of the polynomials.
nodes.statement_short: Discretize the linearized fit with quadrature in monomial coefficients.

nodes.name: Matrix form
nodes.statement:
Let us rewrite~\eqref{eq:minProb} in matrix form, using the notation  egin{align} \mathbf{\Lambda} &= 	ext{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_K),
otag \ \mathbf{\widehat{Q}} &= 	ext{diag}\left[\widehat{Q}(z_1), \widehat{Q}(z_2), \ldots, \widehat{Q}(z_K)ight],
otag \ \mathbf{\widehat{W}} &= 	ext{diag}\left[\widehat{W}(z_1), \widehat{W}(z_2), \ldots, \widehat{W}(z_K)ight],\ V_{kn} &= z_k^n, \quad n=0,1,\ldots,N,
otag \ \mathbf{c} &=  egin{bmatrix} \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{a}\ \end{bmatrix}.
otag \end{align} We obtain,  egin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{c}} \, \left|\left|\mathbf{\Lambda}^ rac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\left[\mathbf{V}, -\mathbf{\widehat{W}}\mathbf{V}ight]\mathbf{c}ight|ight|. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write as a weighted Vandermonde least-squares problem.

nodes.name: Arnoldi bases
nodes.statement: To deal with this problem, we construct two orthonormal bases, one for the column space of $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{V}$ and one for the column space of $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{\widehat{W}V}$. This can be done with the Arnoldi iteration~\cite{arnoldi1951principle,saad2003iterative}, by noting that the columns of $\mathbf{A}$ form a Krylov subspace, \begin{equation} K= \text{span}[\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}^2\mathbf{d}, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}^N\mathbf{d}], \end{equation} where $\mathbf{Z} = \mathrm{diag}\left(z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_K\right)$ and $\mathbf{d} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1})$, and similarly for the columns of $\mathbf{B}$.
nodes.statement_short: Arnoldi orthonormal bases for the Krylov column spaces of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$.

nodes.name: Change of basis
nodes.statement: Once we have constructed the orthonormal bases, \begin{align} \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{P}) &= \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{A}), \quad \mathbf{P^\dagger P} = \mathbf{I} \\ \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{Q}) &= \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{B}), \quad \mathbf{Q^\dagger Q} = \mathbf{I}, \end{align} we rewrite~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete} in the new basis, \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{\tilde{c}}} \, \left|\left|\left[\mathbf{P}, -\mathbf{Q}\right]\mathbf{\tilde{c}}\right|\right|, \end{equation} and impose the normalization condition $\tilde{c}_{2N} = 1$, which corresponds to $Q(z)$ being monic in the new basis.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite in the new bases with $Q$ monic.

nodes.name: Least-squares solve
nodes.statement: The solution of the minimization problem is then obtained by solving the over-determined linear system \begin{equation} [\mathbf{P},-\mathbf{Q}_{1:N-1}]\mathbf{\tilde{c}} = \mathbf{Q}_N \end{equation} in the least-squares sense. In~\eqref{eq:irfLS}, we denote the column corresponding to the $N$th-degree polynomial basis function by $\mathbf{Q}_{N}$, while the rest of the $\mathbf{Q}$ matrix is denoted by $\mathbf{Q}_{1:N-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Overdetermined least-squares solve.

nodes.name: Companion-matrix roots
nodes.statement: Once~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete} is solved, the zeros of $Q(z)$, which are the poles for the next iteration, can be obtained without transforming back to the monomial basis. They are the eigenvalues of a generalized companion matrix~\cite{coelho1999robust}, \begin{equation} \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{H}_{1:N,1:N} - H_{N+1,N}\,\mathbf{\tilde{c}}_{N+1:2N}\,\mathbf{e}_N^T, \end{equation} where $\mathbf{e}_N$ is the $N^\text{th}$ column of the order-$N$ identity matrix and $\mathbf{H}$ is the upper Hessenberg matrix obtained from the Arnoldi iteration used to generate the orthonormal basis for colsp($\mathbf{B}$).
nodes.statement_short: Poles are eigenvalues of a generalized companion matrix from the Arnoldi Hessenberg matrix.
